source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A single-point cane, because it provides enough support for bilateral leg weakness while preserving the smallest possible base of support.","B":"A quad cane, because it is generally preferred over walkers when both lower extremities are weak and substantial stability is required.","C":"A standard walker, because its broad support base is appropriate when bilateral leg weakness creates a need for improved gait stability.","D":"No assistive device, because walking without external support promotes recovery more safely than using a walker in bilateral leg weakness."}}
source_row.rationale: Merck notes that walkers provide greater stability than canes and are particularly appropriate when bilateral leg weakness contributes to fall risk. Option C is correct because a standard walker provides a broad base of support. Option A offers less support with a single-point cane. Option B offers a larger cane base but still less overall support than a walker for substantial bilateral weakness. Option D removes external support despite the stated mobility deficit.
source_row.source_detail: Using a Cane: a cane is appropriate when only a little help with balance/stability or one-sided weakness is needed; with substantial weakness or balance problems, crutches or a walker may be more appropriate. Among the listed options, a walker provides the broadest support for bilateral weakness. MedlinePlus patient instruction reviewed 2025-04-01; current NLM resource rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Basic Care and Comfort: mobility, positioning, skin integrity, elimination and nonpharmacologic comfort activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.stem: A client has significant bilateral lower-extremity weakness and needs an assistive device for ambulation. Which device generally provides the most appropriate base of support among these options?
